"'''She Loves You'''" is a song by the English rock band [[the Beatles]], written by [[John Lennon]] and [[Paul McCartney]] and released as a single in the United Kingdom on 23 August 1963. The single set and surpassed several sales records in the United Kingdom charts, and set a record in the United States as one of the five Beatles songs that held the top five positions in the charts simultaneously, on 4 April 1964. It remains the band's best-selling single in the UK and was the top-selling single of the 1960s there by any artist.<ref>{{cite web |title=Ken Dodd 'third best-selling artist of 1960s' |url=https://www.bbc.com/news/10201932 |work=[[BBC News]] |date=1 June 2010|access-date=7 September 2020}}</ref>

In November 2004, ''[[Rolling Stone]]'' ranked "She Loves You" number 64 on their list of the [[Rolling Stone's 500 Greatest Songs of All Time|500 Greatest Songs of All Time]].<ref name="Rolling Stone">{{cite magazine |magazine=[[Rolling Stone]] |year=2004 |title=500 GREATEST SONGS OF ALL TIME |url=https://www.rollingstone.com/music/lists/the-500-greatest-songs-of-all-time-20110407/the-beatles-she-loves-you-20110525| access-date=4 April 2013}}</ref> In August 2009, at the end of its "Beatles Weekend", BBC Radio 2 announced that "She Loves You" was the Beatles' all-time best-selling single in the UK based on information compiled by the [[Official Charts Company]].

In Canada, the song was included on the album ''[[Twist and Shout (album)|Twist and Shout]]''. In the US, it was the final song on ''[[The Beatles' Second Album]]''.

sections.heading: Composition
Recording
sections.wikitext:
The song was recorded on 1 July 1963, less than a week after it was written, using a two-track recording machine. Documentation regarding the number of takes required and other recording details does not exist. Early takes of the song featured the use of a [[Maestro FZ-1 Fuzz-Tone]] on Harrison's guitar.<ref>{{cite web | url=http://www.beatlesebooks.com/she-loves-you | title="She Loves You" by the Beatles. The in-depth story behind the songs of the Beatles. Recording History. Songwriting History. Song Structure and Style }}</ref> Mixing was carried out on 4 July.{{sfn|Lewisohn|1988|p=32}} Standard procedure at EMI Studios at the time was to erase the original two-track session tape for singles once they had been mixed down to the (usually [[monaural]]) [[master tape]] used to press records. This was the fate of four Beatles songs that were released as two singles: "[[Love Me Do]]", "[[P.S. I Love You (The Beatles song)|P.S. I Love You]]", "She Loves You" and "[[I'll Get You]]". These tracks only exist as a mono master, although several mock-stereo remixes have been made by EMI affiliates worldwide, including a few made in 1966 by Abbey Road engineer [[Geoff Emerick]].<ref>''The Beatles Swan Songs'' {{ISBN|978-0-966-26497-5}} p. 192</ref> A true stereo mix of "She Loves You", created by [[Giles Martin]] using [[machine learning]] technology commissioned by filmmaker [[Peter Jackson]], was released in 2023 as part of the expanded edition of the ''[[1962–1966]]'' compilation album.

The German division of [[EMI]] (the parent of the Beatles' British record label [[Parlophone Records]]) decided that the only way to sell Beatles records in [[Germany]] would be to re-record them in the [[German language]]. The band thought it unnecessary, but were asked by George Martin to comply, recording "[[Komm, gib mir deine Hand / Sie liebt dich|Sie liebt dich]]" on 29 January 1964, along with "Komm, gib mir deine Hand", at the Pathé Marconi Studios in [[Paris]]. They recorded new vocals over the original backing track to "I Want to Hold Your Hand;" "Sie liebt dich" was recorded entirely from scratch.{{sfn|Lewisohn|1988|p=38}} The German lyrics for "Sie liebt dich" were written by [[Camillo Felgen]] under the pseudonym of "Jean Nicolas" (his full name was Camille Jean Nicolas Felgen).<ref>{{cite web |url=https://www.discogs.com/de/release/1823460-Die-Beatles-Komm-Gib-Mir-Deine-Hand-Sie-Liebt-Dich |title=Die Beatles* – Komm, Gib Mir Deine Hand / Sie Liebt Dich |work=discogs.com |access-date=2026-07-11}}</ref>

sections.heading: United Kingdom
United States
Other countries
sections.wikitext:
Unlike Capitol Records' reluctance to proceed with the Beatles in the US, its Canadian subsidiary, Capitol of Canada, went ahead with the group, and "She Loves You" was released there in September 1963.{{sfn|Everett|2001|p=181}} It was played by [[Ontario]] radio station [[CKWS-AM|CKWS]] the next month, and entered the national [[CHUM Chart]] on 2 December 1963.{{sfn|Everett|2001|p=181}}<ref>{{cite web |url=http://www.math.mcgill.ca/rags/music/chum021263chart.htm |title=The earliest(?) chart showing for The Beatles in Toronto |publisher=R A G Seely | access-date=29 December 2012}}</ref> It reached the top five on 23 December,{{sfn|Everett|2001|p=181}} a full month before any Beatles single would do the same in the US charts.{{sfn|Castleman|Podrazik|1975|p=347}} It then spent nine weeks at No. 1 in the early part of 1964.{{sfn|Everett|2001|p=181}}

"She Loves You" became the first Beatles record to sell well in continental Europe and led to a Beatles tour of Sweden in late October 1963.{{sfn|Davies|1968|p=204}} Before the Beatles' breakthrough with "She Loves You", British acts had only managed sporadic successes in continental European markets.

sections.heading: Cultural impact and legacy
sections.wikitext:
"She Loves You" is the song that thrust the Beatles full-scale into the British national spotlight.{{sfn|Davies|1968|p=200}}{{sfn|Lewisohn|1988|p=35}} Part of this was the effectiveness of the song's hook; author Eric Starr wrote in retrospect, "Each chorus or refrain pounds the hook into your head until it's imprinted in your brain."{{sfn|Starr|2007|p=181}} As [[Nicholas Schaffner]] later wrote, it was "'yeah, yeah, yeah' chanted repeatedly and emphatically enough to drive any listener out of his mind, one way or the other."{{sfn|Schaffner|1977|p=22}}

Moreover, it became the signature phrase for the group at the time.{{sfn|Davies|1968|p=200}}{{sfn|Lewisohn|1988|p=35}}{{sfn|Rayl|Gunther|1989|p=10}} The ''[[Daily Mirror]]''{{'}}s approving editorial of 5 November 1963, following the Beatles' acclaimed appearance at the [[Royal Variety Performance]] the night before, was entitled "Yeah! Yeah! Yeah!"{{sfn|Schaffner|1977|p=22}} ''[[The New York Times]]''{{'}} lengthy article of 8 February 1964, describing the frenzy accompanying the group's arrival at [[John F. Kennedy International Airport]] and in New York City, made reference to "Yeah, yeah, yeah" in its first paragraph, continuation headline, and closing paragraph.<ref>{{cite news |url=https://timesmachine.nytimes.com/timesmachine/1964/02/08/106937497.pdf |title=3,000 Fans Greet British Beatles |first=Paul |last=Gardner |author-link=Paul Gardner (journalist) |newspaper=[[The New York Times]] |date=8 February 1964 |page=25}}</ref> An [[Associated Press]] story describing the positive critical reaction to the group's film ''[[A Hard Day's Night (film)|A Hard Day's Night]]'' was headlined "'Yeah, Yeah, Yeah' For Beatles' Film" and labelled "She Loves You" as "the original 'Yeah, Yeah, Yeah,' song".<ref name="ap-stpt-yyy">{{cite news |url=https://news.google.com/newspapers?id=V09SAAAAIBAJ&pg=5987,3837265 |title='Yeah, Yeah, Yeah' For Beatles' Film |agency=[[Associated Press]] |newspaper=[[St. Petersburg Times]] |date=8 July 1964 |page=9A}}</ref>

The phrase became synonymous not just with the Beatles but with the associated kind of popular music overall.{{sfn|Schaffner|1977|p=22}} A ''New York Times'' account describing [[the Animals]]' introductory concert in the city later that year repeated the phrase in description of the group.<ref>{{cite news |url=https://timesmachine.nytimes.com/timesmachine/1964/09/05/97274385.pdf |title=Teen-Agers Howl for the Animals |first=Howard |last=Thompson |author-link=Howard Thompson (film critic) |newspaper=[[The New York Times]] |date=5 September 1964 |page=11}}</ref>

[[Clinton Heylin]] remarked that the chorus "no, no, no" in [[Bob Dylan]]'s 1964 song "[[It Ain't Me, Babe]]" was taken as a parody of the Beatles' "yeah, yeah, yeah" in "She Loves You".<ref>{{cite book |last=Heylin |first=Clinton |author-link=Clinton Heylin |title=Bob Dylan: Behind the Shades Revisited |year=2001 |publisher=HarperCollins |isbn=0-06-052569-X |page=154}}</ref> The melody in both phrases uses a scale descending through a [[minor third]].

In the 22 January 1965, [[The Flintstones|''Flintstones'']] episode "The Hatrocks and The Gruesomes", as new hillbilly neighbors, the "Hatrocks" (who, it is revealed early on, hate 'Bug Music' by 'The Four Insects'—an obvious dig at the Beatles at the time), outgrow their welcome, the Flintstones and Rubbles rig their radio and phone and, wearing Beatle wigs, broadcast a performance of "She Said 'Yeah! Yeah! Yeah!'", driving them out of their house and over to the Gruesomes, who are also performing the song while wearing Beatle wigs.

In 1975, authors [[Roy Carr]] and [[Tony Tyler]] wrote in ''[[The Beatles: An Illustrated Record]]'' that "If a future archivist were to select one single tune to characterise the Beatles' appeal and the stylistic devices for which they became world famous, he would be forced to choose 'She Loves You'."{{sfn|Carr|Tyler|1975|p=20}} In 1979, author [[Greil Marcus]] included "She Loves You" in his ''Stranded: Rock and Roll for a Desert Island'' list of essential rock records.{{sfn|Marcus|1979|p=257}} Even more fundamentally, Marcus posed the question of what one would tell a [[Martian]] who landed and asked the meaning of rock and roll? The first answer would be "She Loves You".{{sfn|Marcus|1979|p=252}}

The British establishment at that time found the refrain "yeah, yeah, yeah" controversial. National radio in the form of the [[BBC]] broadcast the single and "in some quarters it was seen to hail the collapse of civilised society".{{sfn|''Mojo Magazine''|2002|p=60}}

"Yeah, yeah, yeah" was to have a great effect on the Beatles' image – in some parts of [[Europe]], they became known as the ''yeah-yeahs'' or ''yé-yés''.{{sfn|MacDonald|2005|pp=83–85}}

As late as the mid-1970s, some countries in Southeast Asia were still putting out edicts that forbade Beatles haircuts and so-called "yeah, yeah, yeah music".{{sfn|Schaffner|1977|p=22}} Malaysia was an outlier in the region, its media ecosystem encouraging the thriving of Beatles-inspired rock music and giving birth to the ''[[pop yeh-yeh]]'' genre during this period.<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Lockard |first1=Craig A. |title=From Folk to Computer Songs: The Evolution of Malaysian Popular Music, 1930–1990 |journal=The Journal of Popular Culture |date=Dec 1996 |volume=30 |issue=3 |pages=8-9 |doi=10.1111/j.0022-3840.1996.00001.x}}</ref>

In 1965, at the 11th Plenary Meeting of the Central Committee of the [[Socialist Unity Party of Germany]] in the Communist [[German Democratic Republic]], the party's General Secretary [[Walter Ulbricht]] referenced the song in a famous speech about copying culture from the Western world, by using the refrain: "Is it truly the case that we have to copy every dirt that comes from the West? I think, comrades, with the monotony of the yeah, yeah, yeah and whatever it is all called, yes, we should put an end to it".<ref>{{cite book |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=g1MaBwAAQBAJ&q=walter+ulbricht+monotony&pg=PA45 |title=Rockin' the Borders: Rock Music and Social, Cultural and Political Change |date=16 April 2010 |publisher=Cambridge Scholars |isbn=9781443822077 |editor=Björn Horgby, Fredrik Nilsson |language=en}}</ref><ref>{{cite video |url=https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=Q55mQpAGNMc  |archive-url=https://ghostarchive.org/varchive/youtube/20211222/Q55mQpAGNMc |archive-date=2021-12-22 |url-status=live |title=Walter Ulbricht – Yeah Yeah Yeah |language=de |publisher=[[YouTube]] |access-date=29 December 2012}}{{cbignore}}</ref>

British Prime Minister [[Alec Douglas-Home]] made a [[gaffe]] in February 1964: his speechwriters, trying to make him appear in touch with popular culture, wrote him the line, "I'm too modest to claim the country loves us, but you know that can't be bad." However, he appeared not to understand the reference, and actually said, "but you know, err, that can't be too bad."<ref>Sandbrook, Dominic, ''White Heat'' (2006), p. 10.</ref>

On 10 December 1980, following the [[murder of John Lennon]] in [[Manhattan]] two nights previously, British tabloid newspaper ''[[The Sun (United Kingdom)|The Sun]]'' printed the front-page headline "They Loved Him Yeah Yeah Yeah".<ref>{{cite web |url=http://sunheadlines.spreadshirt.co.uk/shop/designs |title=Designs |publisher=Sunheadlines.spreadshirt.co.uk |access-date=24 September 2011 |archive-date=18 October 2012 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20121018151612/http://sunheadlines.spreadshirt.co.uk/shop/designs |url-status=dead }}</ref>

On 27 July 2012, a portion of "She Loves You" as well as footage of the band performing the song was included in a montage of British music during the [[Opening ceremony of the London Olympics|opening ceremony]] of the [[London 2012 Olympic Games]]. In 2018, the music staff of ''[[Time Out London]]'' ranked the song at number 7 on their list of the best Beatles songs.<ref>{{cite web |url=https://www.timeout.com/london/music/the-best-beatles-songs |author=Time Out London Music |title=The 50 Best Beatles songs |website=[[Time Out London]] |date=24 May 2018|access-date=11 December 2018}}</ref>

[[Ozzy Osbourne]] credited the song as the inspiration for him to become a musician.<ref>{{Cite web |last=Farber |first=Jim |date=22 July 2025 |title=Ozzy Osbourne Dead at 76, Just Weeks After Black Sabbath’s Final Concert |url=https://www.billboard.com/music/rock/ozzy-osbourne-death-black-sabbath-7325247/ |access-date=26 July 2025 |website=[[Billboard (magazine)|Billboard]] |language=}}</ref> Osbourne went on to become a co-founding member of [[Black Sabbath]] in 1968, one of the pioneers of the [[Heavy metal music|heavy metal]] genre.<ref name="Larson2004a">{{cite book|author=Tom Larson|title=History of Rock and Roll|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=vGJ7XmA8rjIC&pg=PA183|year=2004|publisher=Kendall/Hunt Pub.|isbn=978-0-7872-9969-9|pages=183–187}}</ref>

sections.heading: Later Beatles use
sections.wikitext:
"She Loves You" was sometimes played by the group during performances on the BBC, and one such recording is included on ''[[On Air – Live at the BBC Volume 2]]'', released in 2013. A concert performance of the song, recorded at the [[Prince of Wales Theatre]], London, on 4 November 1963, for the ''[[Royal Variety Performance]]'', appeared in 1995 on ''[[Anthology 1]]''.

Although not one of the new songs that predominated in their July 1964 film debut ''[[A Hard Day's Night (film)|A Hard Day's Night]]'', it was used as the finale of the concert that closes the movie.<ref name="ap-stpt-yyy" />

"She Loves You" was a staple of the [[set list]] of early Beatles tours, and appeared on ''[[The Beatles at the Hollywood Bowl]]''. By late 1964, it had been dropped in favour of newer songs and the other artists' material that remained in their show.{{sfn|Schaffner|1977|pp=15, 29, 41}}  It did not appear in the group's 1965 or 1966 concert performances.{{sfn|Schaffner|1977|pp=43, 45, 51, 59}}

The Beatles later sang the chorus of "She Loves You" in the long fade-out of "[[All You Need Is Love]]", and a carnival-styled [[Organ (music)|organ]] version of the song is featured in their 1967 television film ''[[Magical Mystery Tour (film)|Magical Mystery Tour]]''.<ref>{{cite web |url=http://www.beatlesinterviews.org/db1967.1125.beatles.html |title=Beatles Interview: In Soho 11/25/1967 |publisher=Beatlesinterviews.org |access-date=10 June 2013}}</ref>

"She Loves You" was included in the Beatles compilation albums ''[[A Collection of Beatles Oldies]]'' (1966, not released in the US), ''[[1962–1966]]'' (1973), ''[[20 Greatest Hits (The Beatles album)|20 Greatest Hits]]'' (1982), ''[[Past Masters, Volume One]]'' (1988), and ''[[1 (The Beatles album)|1]]'' (2000). The song was also included on the American promotional version of the ''Rarities'' album, issued as the bonus disc in the limited edition boxed set ''[[The Beatles Collection]]'', in November 1978. The Capitol Records' US album, ''[[The Beatles' Second Album]]'', on which the song had been featured, was included in the 2004 CD release ''[[The Capitol Albums, Volume 1]]'' and rereleased in 2014, individually and in the boxed set ''[[The U.S. Albums|The US Albums]]''.

"Sie Liebt Dich" was included on both the 1978 British ''[[Rarities (1978 The Beatles album)|Rarities]]'' and the 1980 American ''[[Rarities (1980 The Beatles album)|Rarities]]'' as well as on ''Past Masters, Volume One''.

The 2009 CD rerelease of the Beatles' catalog included "She Loves You" and "Sie Liebt Dich" on ''[[Past Masters]]'' (mono and stereo, respectively) and on ''[[Mono Masters]]'' (mono).

Paul McCartney sang "We love you, yeah, yeah, yeah" at the end of his duet with [[Stevie Wonder]] titled "What's That You're Doing?" from ''[[Tug of War (Paul McCartney album)|Tug of War]]''. McCartney has not played the full song in any of his Wings or solo concert tours, but has replicated its use to end performances of "All You Need Is Love" during his 2011–2012 [[On the Run (Paul McCartney)|On the Run Tour]].
sections.text:
"She Loves You" was sometimes played by the group during performances on the BBC, and one such recording is included on On Air – Live at the BBC Volume 2, released in 2013. A concert performance of the song, recorded at the Prince of Wales Theatre, London, on 4 November 1963, for the Royal Variety Performance, appeared in 1995 on Anthology 1.

Although not one of the new songs that predominated in their July 1964 film debut A Hard Day's Night, it was used as the finale of the concert that closes the movie.

"She Loves You" was a staple of the set list of early Beatles tours, and appeared on The Beatles at the Hollywood Bowl. By late 1964, it had been dropped in favour of newer songs and the other artists' material that remained in their show.{{sfn|Schaffner|1977|pp=15, 29, 41}}  It did not appear in the group's 1965 or 1966 concert performances.{{sfn|Schaffner|1977|pp=43, 45, 51, 59}}

The Beatles later sang the chorus of "She Loves You" in the long fade-out of "All You Need Is Love", and a carnival-styled organ version of the song is featured in their 1967 television film Magical Mystery Tour.

"She Loves You" was included in the Beatles compilation albums A Collection of Beatles Oldies (1966, not released in the US), 1962–1966 (1973), 20 Greatest Hits (1982), Past Masters, Volume One (1988), and 1 (2000). The song was also included on the American promotional version of the Rarities album, issued as the bonus disc in the limited edition boxed set The Beatles Collection, in November 1978. The Capitol Records' US album, The Beatles' Second Album, on which the song had been featured, was included in the 2004 CD release The Capitol Albums, Volume 1 and rereleased in 2014, individually and in the boxed set The US Albums.

"Sie Liebt Dich" was included on both the 1978 British Rarities and the 1980 American Rarities as well as on Past Masters, Volume One.

The 2009 CD rerelease of the Beatles' catalog included "She Loves You" and "Sie Liebt Dich" on Past Masters (mono and stereo, respectively) and on Mono Masters (mono).

Paul McCartney sang "We love you, yeah, yeah, yeah" at the end of his duet with Stevie Wonder titled "What's That You're Doing?" from Tug of War. McCartney has not played the full song in any of his Wings or solo concert tours, but has replicated its use to end performances of "All You Need Is Love" during his 2011–2012 On the Run Tour.

Cover versions
sections.wikitext:
Many artists recorded versions of "She Loves You" in the early 1960s including [[Brenda Lee]], for whom the Beatles had acted as a support act when she headlined a gig at the Star Club in [[Hamburg]], West Germany, in 1962.<ref>{{cite web |author=Pore-Lee-Dunn Productions |url=http://www.classicbands.com/BrendaLeeInterview.html |title=Interview With Brenda Lee |website=Classicbands.com |date=1997-09-24 |access-date=2016-09-27}}</ref> Renamed "He Loves You", it appeared on her 1965 album, ''Top Teen Hits'' (also known as ''Brenda Lee Sings Top Teen Hits'').

English group [[McFly]] released a cover of "She Loves You" as the B-side of their hit "[[That Girl (McFly song)|That Girl]]".  It also appears on their LP ''[[The Greatest Bits: B-Sides & Rarities]]'' which was only available at [[Woolworths (United Kingdom)|Woolworths]] stores in the UK.

Several recording artists included the song on albums made up of nothing but Beatles covers: [[Mary Wells]] in 1965 on her album ''[[Love Songs to the Beatles]]'', where it was also renamed "He Loves You"; bandleader [[Count Basie]] on the 1966 album ''[[Basie's Beatle Bag]]''; and the cartoon group [[the Chipmunks]], whose ''[[The Chipmunks Sing the Beatles Hits]]'' included "She Loves You".<ref>[http://www.allmusic.com/album/mw0000194444 AllMusic: "The Chipmunks Sing the Beatles"]</ref> The Chipmunks later covered the song again on the album ''[[The Chipmunks: Rockin' Through the Decades]]''.

[[Peter Sellers]] recorded six different "speaking" cover versions of the song, using different voices/accents, three of which have been rereleased on the 4-disc collection ''A Celebration of Sellers'':<ref>[https://www.amazon.com/Celebration-Sellers-Peter/dp/B000002SIJ/ref=sr_1_2?ie=UTF8&qid=1521463903&sr=8-2&keywords=A+Celebration+of+Sellers Amazon.com: "A Celebration of Sellers"]</ref>
* Irish (twice, each with a different ending [one extremely sexual<ref>[https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=yYeNU4UqOxc YouTube: Peter Sellers covers The Beatles "She Loves You" Irish version]</ref>])
* Cockney
* "Chinless Wonder"
* Upper-class British<ref>[https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=1sVvOsrU6Aw YouTube: Peter Sellers: She Loves You (Twits Version)]</ref>
* Inspired by ''[[Dr. Strangelove]]''<ref>[https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=ICPmZkK3PaY YouTube: Peter Sellers as Dr. Strangelove covering The Beatle's "She Loves You"]</ref>
sections.text:
Many artists recorded versions of "She Loves You" in the early 1960s including Brenda Lee, for whom the Beatles had acted as a support act when she headlined a gig at the Star Club in Hamburg, West Germany, in 1962. Renamed "He Loves You", it appeared on her 1965 album, Top Teen Hits (also known as Brenda Lee Sings Top Teen Hits).

English group McFly released a cover of "She Loves You" as the B-side of their hit "That Girl".  It also appears on their LP The Greatest Bits: B-Sides & Rarities which was only available at Woolworths stores in the UK.

Several recording artists included the song on albums made up of nothing but Beatles covers: Mary Wells in 1965 on her album Love Songs to the Beatles, where it was also renamed "He Loves You"; bandleader Count Basie on the 1966 album Basie's Beatle Bag; and the cartoon group the Chipmunks, whose The Chipmunks Sing the Beatles Hits included "She Loves You". The Chipmunks later covered the song again on the album The Chipmunks: Rockin' Through the Decades.

Peter Sellers recorded six different "speaking" cover versions of the song, using different voices/accents, three of which have been rereleased on the 4-disc collection A Celebration of Sellers:
* Irish (twice, each with a different ending [one extremely sexual])
* Cockney
* "Chinless Wonder"
* Upper-class British
* Inspired by Dr. Strangelove
